content: The impact of biannual ivermectin-albendazole (IA) mass drug administration (MDA) for lymphatic filariasis (LF) elimination on resource use and cost-effectiveness has not been established. A Markov model was employed to estimate the number of treatments and MDA rounds required under biannual IA compared to annual IA. This model was based on probabilities of achieving five effective rounds and passing pre-transmission assessment surveys (pre-TAS) and TAS evaluations. Each biannual MDA round was assumed to be as effective as an annual MDA round, as supported by prior mathematical model simulations. The model projected that biannual IA would require 15 million more treatments but the same number of MDA rounds compared to annual IA. Additionally, 23 countries were estimated to stop MDA in over 90% of endemic implementation units (IUs) by 2024 under biannual MDA, compared to 2027 under annual IA. Introducing biannual IA in all eligible districts (those currently receiving IA) was projected to save $161 million (13%) in undiscounted economic costs in IA countries. However, from a health system perspective, savings in onchocerciasis co-endemic districts would be negligible or potentially negative due to the need to purchase additional ivermectin treatments for the extra round. The cost-effectiveness of biannual IA remains uncertain due to low certainty in efficacy assumptions applied to the costing model. No studies have assessed the impact of biannual IA on health equity, but it was agreed that there is likely no difference in health equity between biannual and annual IA. Delivering more than one MDA round per year might increase the likelihood of individuals receiving at least one treatment. No published studies have evaluated the acceptability of biannual IA among key stakeholders, such as community drug distributors, health workers, Ministry of Health staff, academic researchers, NGOs, pharmaceutical representatives, and donors. Similarly, no studies have specifically assessed the feasibility of biannual IA compared to annual IA. However, biannual ivermectin distribution for onchocerciasis elimination in some countries demonstrates the feasibility of this strategy. Despite this, most stakeholders considered biannual MDA less feasible than the current annual MDA regimen. The feasibility of implementing biannual IA was deemed variable among stakeholders. There is moderate value in conducting additional studies to determine whether biannual IA is more effective than annual IA. Research is needed to assess whether two MDA rounds per year increase annual population coverage and to evaluate the cost-benefit ratio of increased coverage with additional resource requirements. In areas co-endemic for LF and loiasis, the standard IA MDA strategy is not recommended due to the risk of severe adverse events (SAEs) following ivermectin treatment in individuals with high Loa loa microfilaraemia. A provisional recommendation was developed for biannual or more frequent albendazole MDA with coordinated vector control in such settings. This strategy is currently being implemented in at least one country, demonstrating feasibility and acceptability. Albendazole monotherapy MDA is applied in areas where ivermectin has never been introduced, with or without onchocerciasis co-endemicity. Where ivermectin MDA has occurred, IA regimens can continue under current guidance for onchocerciasis-endemic areas. No direct comparative studies have investigated biannual versus annual albendazole MDA. Observational studies suggest that biannual albendazole MDA is safe and effective, though evidence quality is very low. There were no concerns about health equity between biannual and annual albendazole MDA, and biannual treatment may reach populations unable to participate in a single yearly round. Resource requirements for biannual albendazole MDA are expected to increase in the short term compared to annual MDA. The WHO recommends biannual albendazole MDA rather than annual albendazole MDA in IUs where LF is co-endemic with loiasis and ivermectin has not been distributed. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence until new data become available. Monitoring and evaluation should follow existing WHO guidance, including baseline endemicity surveys, coverage evaluations, and impact assessments after effective MDA rounds. If epidemiological thresholds are not achieved, additional MDA rounds are required before reassessment. The overall quality of evidence for biannual albendazole MDA is very low. No studies have assessed its impact on resource use and cost-effectiveness. Biannual albendazole MDA is being implemented in some LF and loiasis co-endemic countries, demonstrating feasibility and acceptability. Future research comparing biannual and annual albendazole MDA is needed to inform potential revisions to current recommendations. Dissemination of guidelines will occur through the WHO website and other channels to ensure broad accessibility and implementation support.
